title: The Effect of the Minimum Wage on the Fast-Food Industry
research_question: How do increases in the federal minimum wage affect starting wages, wage dispersion, employment levels, and product prices in a low-wage industry? Additionally, to what extent do employers utilize the youth subminimum (training) wage provision, and what factors determine its take-up?
data_description: The authors conducted an original longitudinal telephone survey of fast-food restaurants (Burger King, Wendy's, and Kentucky Fried Chicken outlets, sampled from Yellow Pages metropolitan listings) in Texas. The first wave was administered in December 1990 (167 responses, 57% response rate) and the second wave between July 8 and August 2, 1991 (330 responses, 56% response rate; 110 restaurants matched across waves). A reliability re-interview of 30 restaurants was conducted in August 1991. Variables collected include starting wages for part-time and full-time nonmanagement workers (both retrospective pre-increase and current), full-time and part-time employment counts, prices of standard items (medium soda, small fries, basic hamburger or six-piece chicken), worker demographics (share Hispanic, share black, share teenage), ownership type (company-owned vs. franchise), chain affiliation, and fringe benefits. Local labor market characteristics (city unemployment rate, population) were merged from the County and City Data Book, 1988. The unit of observation is the individual restaurant establishment.
institutional_context: After nearly a decade with the federal minimum wage frozen at $3.35, amendments to the Fair Labor Standards Act raised it to $3.80 on April 1, 1990, and to $4.25 on April 1, 1991. The legislation also introduced a youth subminimum (training) wage allowing employers to pay teenage workers 85% of the minimum wage (initially $3.35, then $3.62) for up to six months. Texas was selected because it has many low-paid workers, average retail and teenage wages below national averages, a high share of teens earning near the old minimum, and no binding state minimum wage. The fast-food industry was chosen because it is highly competitive, has high turnover, hires many first-time and teenage workers, and is heavily constrained by the minimum wage—roughly one-third of sampled restaurants paid exactly the minimum before April 1990, rising to over three-quarters paying exactly $4.25 after April 1991—making it a setting where minimum wage effects should be especially visible.
